chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Sahl ibn Ziyad, all from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abi Basir from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

"If a man who is poor (mu'sir) is Hajj-ed by another man, it counts as one Hajj for him. If he becomes wealthy after that, Hajj is incumbent upon him. And likewise the Nasib (one who bears enmity), when he gains knowledge, Hajj is incumbent upon him, even if he has already performed Hajj." What this hadith included from his saying 'And likewise the Nasib, when he gains knowledge, Hajj is incumbent upon him' is to be taken as recommended (istihbab), because whenever he performs Hajj while being a mu'talif (opponent), that suffices for him for the Hajj of Islam. That which indicates this is what he narrated:

key_terms.أَجْزَأَهُ: It sufficed for him / was accepted for him
key_terms.الاسْتِحْبَاب: Recommended (a level of legal ruling below obligation)
key_terms.النَّاصِب: The Nasib, one who bears enmity (specifically towards the Ahl al-Bayt)
key_terms.مُعْسِر: A person who is poor or unable to afford Hajj

ai.seo_question: Does a poor person who has Hajj paid for for them need to perform another Hajj if they become wealthy?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi cites this narration to elucidate the principle of *Hajjat al-Islam* (the obligatory Hajj), noting that a poor person’s Hajj paid by another counts as their single duty, yet wealth acquisition later triggers a new obligation. The text extends this logic to the *Nasib* (enemies of the Ahl al-Bayt), suggesting that if their prior Hajj was performed while in a state of enmity, acquiring knowledge of the truth makes a new Hajj incumbent upon them, though the scholar notes this may be interpreted as recommended (*mustahabb*) since the previous act still discharged the basic duty. This highlights the Shia juristic view that spiritual status and financial capacity jointly determine the recurrence of the Hajj obligation.
